pr_comments: I split out a bunch of commits into their own PRs now, so that they can be review/merged more quickly.

Two notes:

1. I noticed that the ExecStatus structs embedded into ExecCommand aren't actually serialized properly. exit/status/timestamps are flushed out on reload. That sucks.

2. While this collects the timestamps now for all unit types, all service types, and all commands, this is not generally exposed on D-Bus, since D-Bus is so nasty to extend for this, and we already did this once and it wasnt fun. I did expose it fully in the state "dump" and it's quite interesting there. we should look into exposing this via D-Bus later. or maybe alternatively don't bother, and focus on exposing this only via Varlink, since it's so much easier there to expose it.

It's fine to have the infrastructure in place, but won't hooking it up everywhere cause _a lot_ of additional back and forth on the main event loop? Every time a control process or a oneshot or a socket or anything else gets triggered, it's additional work and message processing, and it's all for stats that are not actually published. Wouldn't it be better to keep the infra in place, but do not enable it until a request to do so comes in?

> It's fine to have the infrastructure in place, but won't hooking it up everywhere cause _a lot_ of additional back and forth on the main event loop? Every time a control process or a oneshot or a socket or anything else gets triggered, it's additional work and message processing, and it's all for stats that are not actually published. Wouldn't it be better to keep the infra in place, but do not enable it until a request to do so comes in?

This stuff is processed asynchronously with a large queue. Also, grepping through the units files we ship it doesn't add more traffic over your approach, maybe 50% more or so, and that's easily processed. It's in other ways a bit more efficient, since we only need to process a single AF_UNIX SOCK_DGRAM socket over a larger number of per-unit fifos.

As usual: if this becomes a problem in real-life we can revisit anything, but right now i see no reason to believe passing the same socket fd to all forked off processes would be in any worse than allocating/passing an exec_fd to just the majority of services.

comments: It's about service activation tracking, so moving it to a different place is enough, which is not an API but just an internal rearrangement so no need to block rc
well, my think was that it actually would be nice to track this for all forked processes, and in that case it would probably have to change name

ExecMain timestamps are for the main processes already. It would require a new and separate exec_fd, which means there won't be a single last-thing-to-do-before-execve anymore, but two of them, which will race each other. If there's no use case for it, let's not make things more complicated for no benefit.

> ExecMain timestamps are for the main processes already. It would require a new and separate exec_fd, which means there won't be a single last-thing-to-do-before-execve anymore, but two of them, which will race each other. If there's no use case for it, let's not make things more complicated for no benefit.

I don't see a race there? how would there be a race?

sure you have to decide what to do first, i.e. take/send the timestamp or mark the execfd as "hot", but that's fine. neither of these are "risky" or "slow" operations, hence just do one first, doesn't really matter which one you pick.

review_comments:
Hmm, I don't think Exit timestamp should be switched to only show delta?

The point of handoff timestamp is to measure the sd-executor latency and such, and that ought to be an extremely short period, hence it makes sense to only show timespan for that. But that reasoning doesn't apply to the exit timestamp?

well, i agree, but the way i understood @keszybz is that he doesn't want to see the calendar time again.

at this point i really don't care anymore, let's just get this merged, i'll change the timestamp display on this to anything people are happy with. 

i am happy to drop that commit btw, if it's so hard to agree on an outout acceptable to everyone.

Thanks for adding the pre-exec failure case - the post-exec failure case that was covered here is still missing though. IE, if sighup comes and the logic was disabled, the metric needs to be reset too

but why? i think it's really interesting to know when the handoff was attempted, even if it failed later. why hide the timestamp? 

that the handoff failed is recorded, hence if clients want to ignore the timestamp in that case they can suppress it. But i think it's valuable to collect the handoff attempt time either way.

I mean, this is generally what logging does: it collects not just info about things that failed, but also *when* they failed. Hence, here, for tracking activation results I also think it's highly interesting to know *when* the handoff failed if it failed.

If this was a log then of course you'd be right - but it isn't, it's a metric, which is subtly different in that it has a semantic meaning. And the meaning is: we gave this to the kernel at this time, not our job anymore. But in this failure case that _doesn't happen_, so it's just confusing to have the metric be available for an event that did not actually happen, and it remains our job to handle it - with retries or with failure reporting depending on configuration.

Having a log message in addition, that is always reported regardless, would be of course good for me to have, on top of the separate metric. Then, you always get the reporting of the attempt with the messaged timestamp in the logs, but the metric's meaning remains the same.
Sorry, but i just disagree. The data is relevant either way. There's really no need to suppress it.

It's not relevant for the actual use case, as it changes the meaning to something different, as explained. How about adding a log message, so that you get the data, and resetting the metric, so that it keeps the meaning it was added for? Best of both worlds and we can move on.
I think it's better to take the timestamp in all cases. The timestamp is a piece of information that is independent of whether the exec succeeded.
Taken and sent back and logged sure, but I'd like it to be reset in the public API, as in, the new dbus property, for the reasons already explained

@poettering this is still outstanding, which I gather means you have no intention of fixing as asked. That's fine, but could you please at least document the behaviour in `man/org.freedesktop.systemd1.xml` so that there are no surprises?

Then I'll approve. Thanks.
